Create Connection Manager Group
A Connection Manager Group organises one or more lightweight relays on your network. Guardian sends agentless scans through them to reach targets over WinRM (Windows) or SSH (Linux/macOS) — nothing is installed on the nodes themselves.
Group created
Install a Connection Manager below to activate this group.
Group created — use these credentials to install
API key:grd_k8x…generated
Guardian URL:https://guardian.cloudhouse.com
Choose installer
Run this command on the host where you want to install the Connection Manager:
powershell
irm https://guardian.cloudhouse.com/cm/install.ps1 | iex
Installation requirements
• Supported OS: Windows Server 2019+ or Linux (RHEL/Ubuntu) 64-bit
• Admin permissions: local admin or sudo
• Network: outbound HTTPS 443 to Guardian, WinRM 5985/5986 or SSH 22 to targets
• Guardian URL must be reachable from the host

One-time setup in your AWS account. Enter your account ID above, then create an OIDC identity provider and an IAM role from the values below and paste the role ARN back here. Guardian exchanges a short-lived OIDC token for STS credentials — no long-lived keys are stored.
Step 1 — Add an OIDC identity provider (IAM → Identity providers → Add provider → OpenID Connect)
https://static.cloudhouse.com
sts.amazonaws.com
Step 2 — Create an IAM role with this trust policy (IAM → Roles → Create role → Custom trust policy)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/static.cloudhouse.com" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "static.cloudhouse.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
          "static.cloudhouse.com:sub": "guardian-service/acme-corp"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
The trust policy only controls who may assume the role. Also attach a permission policy (e.g. SecurityAudit or ReadOnlyAccess) granting the AWS actions Guardian scans with.
ARN of the role you created above. Guardian assumes it via web-identity to run discovery and scans.
One-time setup in your AWS account. Create an IAM user with a read-only policy and a role Guardian can assume, then paste the access key and role ARN below.
Set up in AWS (IAM Console)
1 · Create an IAM user
Programmatic access only — no console access. Name it Guardian. Permissions are attached in step 4.
2 · Create a read-only IAM policy GuardianReadOnlyAccess
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "GuardianReadOnly",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:Describe*", "ec2:GetConsoleOutput",
        "ecs:ListClusters", "ecs:DescribeClusters",
        "eks:ListClusters", "eks:DescribeCluster",
        "rds:DescribeDBInstances", "rds:DescribeDBClusters",
        "lambda:ListFunctions", "lambda:GetFunction",
        "s3:ListAllMyBuckets", "s3:GetBucketPolicy",
        "iam:GetUser", "iam:GetRole",
        "sts:GetCallerIdentity", "sts:GetAccessKeyInfo"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
3 · Create an IAM role GuardianRole with this trust policy
Custom trust policy, so the Guardian user can assume the role. On the permissions step, attach GuardianReadOnlyAccess.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/Guardian" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
4 · Let the user assume the role inline policy: GuardianAssumeRole
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/GuardianRole"
    }
  ]
}
5 · Create access keys
Use case "Application running outside AWS". Copy the key ID and secret — the secret is only shown once.
Guardian uses the access key to assume this role for discovery and scanning.
IAM Permissions required
ec2:Describe*
ecs:List*
eks:Describe*
lambda:List*
rds:Describe*

Configure Secret Server
Connect Guardian to your Secret Server so agentless scans can pull credentials at scan time
Secret Server
Delinea / Thycotic credential manager
A label for this connection. Defaults to a sensible name — change it if you connect more than one.
The base URL of your Secret Server instance.
Service account with access to credential storage.
Stored encrypted; used to obtain an OAuth2 token.
Secret folder paths
Full path of the folder(s) that hold the secrets Guardian may use — e.g. \Personal Folders\Guardian. Secrets in these folders appear when you pick a credential for a node.
Authentication method
How Guardian authenticates to Secret Server. Username & password is supported today — other methods are on the roadmap.
Guardian requests an OAuth2 token using the service account above (username & password), then uses it as a bearer token for all Secret Server API calls. No further setup needed.
Coming soon
Authenticate with a Secret Server application API key instead of a service-account password — no password stored in Guardian.

Connection & Credentials
How Guardian will reach these nodes when you scan them
Unlike cloud discovery, ServiceNow nodes are scanned over WinRM/SSH through a Connection Manager. Pick one below and set the credentials those scans should use — you can change them per node later.
Connection Manager Required
The relay that reaches these nodes on your network.
Default credentials
Recommended. Applied to every imported node of each type, so scans work as soon as you promote them. Credentials usually come from Secret Server, or enter them directly.
Windows nodes · WinRM
credentials for all detected Windows nodes
Fetched at scan time. Manage connections in .
No default set. You can add Windows credentials later — per node, or in bulk from the Detected tab.
Linux / macOS nodes · SSH
credentials for all detected Linux & macOS nodes
Fetched at scan time. Manage connections in .
No default set. You can add Linux/macOS credentials later — per node, or in bulk from the Detected tab.
Credentials are fetched at scan time, never stored in plain text

Change Reconciliation Active ✓
ServiceNow is syncing change requests automatically — reconciliation runs in the background
Auto-sync running · company.service-now.com · Every 15 min

How automated reconciliation works
CRs sync automatically from ServiceNow
Every 15 minutes · All open change requests pulled · Matched to Guardian nodes via CMDB CI ID
Guardian captures scans before & after change windows
Baseline snapshot before window opens · Post-change scan when window closes · Requires time to complete
3
Change lifecycle completes in ServiceNow
Approval, implementation, review & closure · This phase may take hours or days depending on your process
4
Reconciliation results appear in Changes tab
Guardian auto-reconciles each CR · Matched, partial or unmatched · Full audit trail logged
Currently Tracked CRs (47 synced) Future CRs only
Matched = all linked nodes in Guardian Partial = some nodes missing
Only CRs with a planned start after reconciliation was enabled are tracked. Past/retroactive changes are excluded.

CHG0012345 Kernel update — web-prod-01 web-prod-01, web-prod-02 ● Matched Tomorrow 02:00–04:00
CHG0012346 SSL cert renewal api-server-01 ● Matched Tomorrow 03:00–05:00
CHG0012347 Security patch ecs-cluster-prod ● Matched Thu 22:00–23:00
CHG0012348 Config change — eks-prod eks-prod, eks-staging ● Partial Fri 01:00–02:00
Automated reconciliation is on/off — you cannot select individual changes. Be aware that a change may be auto-reconciled against a CR even if the actual change that occurred does not match what the CR describes — for example, if a node was listed in the CR but the specific change was unrelated. Review flagged items in the Detected Drift tab to catch mismatches.
Manual reconciliation is also available from the Detected Drift tab for immediate results or when automated integration is not active.
